utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's have appearances for today starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning Your Honours counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution Daryl Mundis and Kyle Wood assisted by our case manager Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution, to everyone in the courtroom and around it. My name is Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. Robson I appear on behalf of General Delic. With us this morning is our legal assistant Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I notice the witness is not in court. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to ask for a few minutes to address you before we let the witness enter the courtroom. I have a few questions to raise, and I wanted to state those for the record by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first issue has to do with the witness that is to testify tomorrow. It was foreseen that the witness will testify tomorrow. On the 26th of February, 2007, we received an audio recording of this witness's interview from the OTP. It was taken with the -- with an investigator on the 22nd of January, 2007. We immediately noticed that it was an incomplete recording and we asked the Prosecutor to forward a full interview. The Prosecutor told us that there was a mistake made when recording and that one part of the interview is missing due to technical difficulties. A few days ago, that is on the 14th of September this year, I believe it was last Friday, we received the complete transcript or at least what should be the complete transcript of the interview in English and Bosnian. It is clearly visible that a portion of the interview is missing. I personally went through the transcript, and I was able to see the following: At page 8 out of 27, lines 30 to 35 of tape 6601-1-A, the Prosecutor clearly mentions a previous meeting with the witness, and he also states that there were notes taken on that occasion. Then on page 2, line 25 -- sorry, page 2 of 25, tape 6602-1-B, lines 21 to 28, the witness mentions having met an investigator in October 2006. And he also states that he expected a -- his statement typed out by the investigator. He was promised such a copy but never got one. On the next page of the same tape the investigator told the witness that he can provide a CD-ROM with his October interview. Your Honour, I would believe you will remember that I raised the issue of all previously given statements by all witnesses. I raised that on several occasions, including at the Pre-Trial Conference. In this case I requested to receive the entire statement as I did in all other cases. However, we still didn't receive that. What I wanted to stress is the following, and it is particularly worrying to me. That is why I raised this issue in the first place. At the very end of the transcript of the interview and the last sentence concluding the transcript of the audio recording we requested, the investigator told the witness the following my English is far from perfect but I wanted to quote that witness: "[In English] We agreed on Tuesday, you can't come tomorrow because I remember that you said -- okay. We can stop it now. We can do these things. It doesn't have to be on the tape these things. First we stop the tape." [Interpretation] And then the time entered for the conclusion of the conversation. We also receive a note stating that there are four tapes that cannot be heard. Your Honour, I am very worried with the things that seem to be taking place and what those things are that are discussed with the witness and were not being recorded. We cannot receive that portion of the tape and, therefore, we cannot prepare for our cross-examination. What is very significant and indicative in this transcript is the following: I know that you received witness statements, and I hope you will be able to see what the modus used is. It is clearly visible that the investigator is arguing with the witness throughout, instructing him to repeat something that's stated in the previous statement. I insist upon receiving this statement, and I wanted to state for the record that I cannot approach any cross-examination of this witness before being given both the transcript and the full audio recording of the missing tapes. In this case and in all other cases such as this one, I cannot begin my cross-examination unless I have all of the relevant material mentioned by the witness. It is the basic right of the accused and his Defence to be able to confront the witness and put that -- any given witness to the -- any given statement to the witness here in the trial. This was not the only case, Your Honour, and for the future I will -- seems I will seek to raise objections to any and every such instances. Another issue is something that has to do with certain comments made by the Prosecutor outside the courtroom. On Friday, at the end of the session I was informed by Mr. Mundis of the existence of an alleged video recording of Delic's address to the El Mujahid detachment. For me as well as for Mr. Mundis, this was something quite customary. Mr. Mundis and I thought we would be able to deal with this question within the framework of the regular existing procedure that is to be put in place during the proceedings. However, the very same day the spokesperson of Mrs. Del Ponte, Mrs. Olga Kavran, gave a statement that has to do with that alleged piece of evidence which was carried by literally all the media in Bosnia, Croatia, and Montenegro as well as Serbia. I received 27 phone calls from journalists regarding that. The titles read: "Proof of Delic's guilt," in that statement. That is why I am addressing you now. She comments on the recording which seems to be an alleged proof of Delic's address to the Mujahedin at their farewell. According to her statement, it is said that several witnesses spoke on that in the proceedings. We were all aware of these proceedings. At this moment it is far less significant for me that she gave an incorrect statement. However, what is very detrimental and inappropriate is that the Prosecutor, Carla Del Ponte, through her spokesperson, provides statements on certain witnesses in this case outside the courtroom. I believe such statements to a great extent damage the integrity of these proceedings. Such comments cause bias and prejudice in the public concerning Mr. Delic's guilt, and far worse they endanger the possibility to have a fair trial. Such a statement on the part of the Prosecutor I am certain managed to reach all the Prosecutor's witnesses in the region since it was carried in the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serbia, Montenegro, and Croatia. It's been going on for three days. There was not a single TV station that did not broadcast that. Not only is it that such comments can have an impact on the witnesses, it also has additional effects on the public. That is why I wish the Chamber to order the Prosecution to refrain from such comments in the future. I myself behaved in the way so far that any matter regarding these proceedings have to be discussed only in this courtroom. We are not allowed to discuss any evidence publicly. As soon as General Delic heard about his indictment, he came to confront it here in this courtroom. However, we cannot fight what is going on outside the courtroom. Ms. Del Ponte should do what her job is, and she should take care of the people who are to blame for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people. What we have to do, however, here in this courtroom is to deal with our evidence. Another issue, Your Honour -- I wanted to state another thing for the transcript, and I want to do that each and every time before a given witness comes in. I want to contest the authenticity of document P2761. I had the occasion to speak with the author of this document, and I will address the document much more extensively during cross-examination with the witnesses. For the time being I just wanted to have the transcript record my objection as to the authenticity, and I wish to be able to be given an opportunity to inspect the original of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Madam Vidovic, this document P267, has it already been tendered into evidence or is it still to come?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is document P2761. It is possible, Your Honour. It is P2761. I think it was admitted. However, late last night I had this discussion with the author of the document, and the system was not operational. That's another thing. I have to complain to you by saying that the system that is used by the Defence is inoperative on weekends often, and it was only last night that I learned from the author, because he was absent from Bosnia-Herzegovina for a long time, that there may be issues as to the authenticity. That is why I raise it here before we have the witness. I will double-check, however, on the exact designation of the exhibit. It is possible it has been admitted. My assistant is telling me that she managed to verify already that it is Exhibit 111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. That's all I wanted to find out about the document Okay. You have raised three issues, Madam Vidovic. Do you have any specific relief you would like to ask for with respect to either each or all of them? Very briefly. I did hear that you -- you said that with the first issue you will not cross-examine the witness unless for the full statement. The second issue you said the Prosecution must be warned not to make these statements outside, and the other one, of course, is saying you're going to challenge the authenticity. Of those, do I summarise you correctly? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour, save for the first request. It also has to do with the fact that I cannot begin my cross-examination without having been given a previous statement which seems to be in existence. It is dated October 2006. The rest is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, do you have any response to what we have talked about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Just very briefly with respect to the witness who is scheduled to appear tomorrow. We will make inquiries as to this prior statement that Ms. Vidovic is has referred to and whether or not there is in fact a witness statement or notes and whether that material has in fact been disclosed, and we will inform the Trial Chamber as soon as we're able to make those queries and find out some additional information, and if there is material to be disclosed I assure you it will be disclosed as quickly as possible. With respect to the recorded interview of February 2007 that Ms. Vidovic refers to, that recorded interview took seven tapes and there were seven tapes that recorded that interview. Two of those seven tapes are in fact inaudible. There is -- the quality of the sound on those tapes renders it impossible to provide a transcript, and I believe, with all due respect to my learned colleague, that that is perhaps what she's referring to when she says the transcript is incomplete or there's material that's not available. All seven of those tapes have been disclosed, but I repeat that on two of those seven tapes the quality of the recording renders it such that it was impossible for the transcription and translation departments to hear anything on those two tapes in order to produce a transcript. So that is a technical impossibility for us to provide a transcript or a translation of that transcript simply because the quality of the tape is such that nothing can be heard on two of those seven tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you on that point? Am I correct to assume that in fact the Defence is not only given a transcript but also the audiotapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. If a -- if an interview -- if the Prosecution conducts a recorded interview, whether it's audiotapes or videotapes, those tapes are provided to the Defence as well as a transcript of that recorded interview and a translation thereof if required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So if an audio or videotape is inaudible and incomprehensible but it's -- the entire tape is given to the Defence, the Defence should be able to determine for themselves that in fact nothing can be heard from that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the second point concerning the emergence late last week of an alleged recording of the accused speaking at the Mujahedin farewell, the Prosecution has nothing further at this point to add, and I think that we'll just leave that as it is at the moment. Undoubtedly there will be further developments with respect to this alleged recording, but at this point in time we have nothing to add other than my understanding that the Prosecutor's spokesperson was referring to the evidence, in fact, that has been led of such a meeting, and we believe that witnesses have testified in open court about the attendance at that farewell meeting of the accused, and I'll leave that as it is. I don't believe that -- that we have any further comments with respect to the third point. The document that Ms. Vidovic is challenging on authenticity grounds is in fact in evidence, and we'll leave that up to the Defence and the Trial Chamber with respect to any future action that they may wish to take with respect to that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I notice you are standing up, Madam Vidovic. Let me just get clarity from you. This audiotape or statement that you received from February last year, is it incomplete because you cannot hear part of the tape or is it incomplete because some tapes have not been provided?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the statement is incomplete for the reasons stated by Mr. Mundis. We cannot hear. However, that is not the issue at hand. The issue is the one I shared with you. The Prosecutor says: [In English] These things, it doesn't have to be on the tape these things." [Interpretation] In other words, it means that we have what we have, and we'll use the framework provided. However, there are things done that are not on the tape. That is in the February 2007 statement. I want to receive the full statement that had been given October, and the investigator keeps arguing with the witness about that statement. The witness repeatedly says that he wants to see the statement and he is denied. Therefore the problem is the previous statement, I do not believe that the Prosecutor will go beyond the scope of the statement that we received. We both have it. What we have on the transcript we have, but we want to have the notes about what is not in the transcript. The Prosecutor says that they will be discussing other things. I don't know what those other things are that are done with witnesses that are not on the tape and not part of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. Is it the Prosecutor saying they were discussing other things or is it the investigate? This transcript says Prosecutor and the translation said Prosecutor. Sorry, just read this last paragraph, Madam Vidovic. You're saying the Prosecutor says they will be discussing other things. "I don't know what those other things are that are done with witnesses that are not on the tape and not part of the interview." Did you mean to say investigator or did you -- you've got to be clear who -- who you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was talking of Michael Koehler, investigator of the OTP who says, [In English] We can stop it now. We can do these things. It doesn't have to be on the tape these things." That is the problem. I want to see what those things are. I want a note on that and the previous statement given in October, because the investigator keeps arguing about it with the witness. He also promised to provide it to the witness, and we, the Defence, never received a recording of that statement. That is completely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. I think I understand your point now. Mr. Mundis, are you able to respond specifically to the statement that is allegedly said -- that says, "We don't have to talk about these things. We don't have to put them on tape," and also about the previous statement that has not been disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I -- as I've indicated earlier, I will -- or I'm in the process of making these inquiries and will get back to the Trial Chamber as soon as possible. I am not aware of any written, signed statement from October 2006. It's possible that Mr. Koehler met with the witness in October, perhaps spoke with him, perhaps took some notes, perhaps then indicated we need to have a more full interview at a subsequent date which was then done in February 2007. That is entirely possible. We will attempt to locate those notes or if there was a written statement that was signed by the witness, we will locate that and disclose it as soon as possible. With respect to the statement about certain things not being needed to be done on the tape, I would need to review the transcript, perhaps the preceding portion of the transcript. I don't know what Mr. Koehler was referring to. Quite often witnesses show up with documents and the documents are then handed over and perhaps Mr. Koehler is referring to that not needing to be on the tape. I simply don't know what Mr. Koehler said in the few minutes preceding that part which Ms. Vidovic has read out to us. I don't have the transcript in front of me. I will make the inquiries and get back to the Chamber as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On this first issue, the issue of that statement of the witness, are we likely not to proceed with the witness tomorrow because of these difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would -- I would think, Your Honours, that even if there were to be, and I stress even if there were to be any issue concerning perhaps delayed disclosure or disclosure in issue, we could certainly do the direct examination, and if need be bring the witness back at a subsequent time for cross-examination or perhaps depending on -- if there is material to be disclosed, how lengthy it is, perhaps Ms. Vidovic could do her cross-examination the day after tomorrow. Again, the witness is scheduled to be here tomorrow and the following day, so I simply don't know if there is material to be disclosed, and if there is material how much material there is, but we would certainly be in a position to do -- to conduct the direct examination tomorrow and take it as far as we possibly could in the event there was additional material that needed to be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the event there was any material to disclose, would it make sense for the Prosecution to lead and for Madam Vidovic to cross-examine on a subsequent date or would it be better for the witness just to be postponed and come back on a subsequent date so that both his or her evidence in chief and cross-examination are at one place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would be in these circumstances obviously in the Trial Chamber's hands. If the Trial Chamber would prefer to hear the witness in one sitting, we will send the witness home and bring him back at a later point in time. I will indicate that the witness schedule for Thursday and Friday would be unlikely that we could move him up, in which case we would do the witness that's here today. I expect him to go into tomorrow and then we would most likely adjourn early tomorrow, not sit on Wednesday, and then resume on Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. It doesn't seem like there is any ruling that is being called for and that the issues have been placed on the record and we can deal with as they unfold. Shall I repeat myself? The transcript seems to have picked me up. I was just saying that it doesn't seem like there is any ruling that is being called for and that the issues have been placed on the record and we can deal with them as they unfold. Shall we leave it at that then, Madam Vidovic, and deal with them as they come up? We will see what develops on the statements is then as stated on the February -- of October 2006, and those statements that are supposed to have been said about not putting things on tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, provided that I receive that statement either today or tomorrow or within a reasonable time. Then I would be able to go through the statement for the sake of both the witness and the Chamber. However, I do wish to see that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If there is a statement, as Mr. Mundis says. He doesn't know whether there is. He is not aware of the statement of October 2006. So if there is no statement, obviously you will get no statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, to clarify one thing, it is fully clear from the transcript that there is a recording of the conversation between the witness and the investigator in October 2006. I want that recording whether the witness signed it or not. I still believe it is the right of this Defence to hear that recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again for the record I am not disputing if there is material it will be disclosed. If there isn't, then there's nothing for me to disclose. I'm not disputing the right of the Defence to have any such material that's in our possession. That's not the issue. The issue is whether there is any such material. If there is, it will be disclosed. If there's not, then obviously it's a non-issue, but I will, as I've said several times, we're making inquiries as I stand here, and whatever we determine, if there is material to be disclosed it will be disclosed, full stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Okay. I think we'll end this discussion at that point. Are you ready to call your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please for the record state your name, date of birth, and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Kadir Jusic. I was born on -- in the Veliki Badic village of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa on the 28th of August, 1948.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What is your occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm retired now. Before that I was a professional soldier, an officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what army were you most recently serving in, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last army that I served in is the army of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and before that in the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Is that the extent of your military experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to the period of 1992 to 1995. Before that I was a member of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, from 1971 when I graduated from the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What was your position in 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1995 I held the duty in the army of BiH in the 3rd Corps. I was chief of staff of the 3rd Corps, of the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And, sir, if you could tell the Trial Chamber is the municipality of Zavidovici in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some more questions about the 3rd Corps now. Who was the commander of the 3rd Corps when you joined in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1995 in March I was appointed chief of staff, and the corps commander was Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown Exhibit 2972, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Sir, do you see that document before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that this order came from the General Staff to the command of the 3rd Corps, and this is that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible to highlight it so that we can be able to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes. If it could be scrolled down a little bit. And actually, move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let us eliminate one point which is not clear. It entered the transcript as prompted by the Prosecutor about Exhibit 2972. I do believe that this is not an exhibit, because this is a document from the Prosecution, and this number may be assigned to another document, but let it be clear that this is P02972, document P02972.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood. May I remind you that when we talk of exhibits, we refer to exhibits that have been admitted into evidence already. Any document that is not yet admitted into evidence is not an exhibit. So please do not characterise such documents as -- as exhibits. We've talked about it. I know it was in your absence in court here before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, and I appreciate my learned colleagues correction on this point. I am referring in fact to P02972, and I make no characterisation intentionally that this has been as yet admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Turning back to the document, if you could -- I draw you're attention, please, to number 1, sir. What is the effect of -- what is the effect of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: -- what's written under number 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an order whereby tasks are being given that will should be carried out with the goal of establishing and re-establishing units, and under this item it is referred to the 35 -- 35th Division command within the 3rd Corps area. So it goes for the tasks that are -- should be -- that are to be carried out with the aim of streamlining the operations as per the estimate of the General Staff that there needs to be some tasks to reorganise the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And if we could go to the next page, and if you could read in particular item 2(a).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we looking at restructuring and renaming?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I didn't go through each and every detail, but more or less I know what this is about. The essence is that certain units that had the certain names that indicated their belonging to another corps, primarily the units within the 37th Brigade, they were to be renamed so as to belong to the 3rd Corps. The former 203rd Brigade of the 2nd Corps was to be renamed the 375th Brigade. The figure 2 means that they were attached to the 2nd Corps, which was the initial establishment that was set up when the corps were being formed. When Tesanj and the other units mentioned here were still in the zone of responsibility of the 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: As to the units listed in 2(a), sir, is this consistent with what you remember of the structure of the corps in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Finally if I could go to the second to last page of this document. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what this is, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the organisational chart of the 3rd Corps. The names of the units as well as the names of commanders and chiefs of staff at the level of the corps, division, and brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I interrupt? Are these two documents the same, the one in English and the other one in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The -- if I could explain. I believe the structure in the English translation is different just so that the words could be bigger and they could be read more easily, but the Prosecution's confident that what is reflected in the translation is in fact what is in the chart itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, if I could draw your attention to the top box there. It appears to include the name Kadir Jusic. Is that you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is me. I was the only person with that first and last name there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what does it indicate that your name's below that of the corps commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means that the corps commander was the first person mentioned there, and then the chief of staff in terms of hierarchy is the second highest ranking person in the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Also, if you could follow the line down there appears to be a line straight from the 3rd Corps Zenica going down to a number of units starting with 303 and going on to 314. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber what it means that the line for these units goes directly to the box marked 3 Corps Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means that those units were directly subordinated to the corps command. Those were the 303rd, 314th, 330th, and the El Mujahid detachment. That was in January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So if we follow that through then, Mr. Jusic, would that -- would it follow then that those units that are listed under the 35th Division box or the 37th Division box are subordinated directly to those larger formations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not a standard chart. I don't know why it was drawn in this way, whether the solid line should only connect the 35th, to the 35th and the 37th Division. The rest should be separated from the line connecting the corps command and the division command. The other line should be separate as for the units subordinate to divisions. This chart is not done professionally, to the extent that the line referred to should not go directly to the 3rd Corps command. In principle, the 3rd Corps command did not command, and there was no need for it to command to the units which were part of individual divisions. It was the divisional command duty. The line should have only gone to the divisions but not -- and the lines are specified directly under the 3rd Corps, however, not the rest. Technically speaking, the chart is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If we could go back, and with apologies, to page 3 of the exhibit, I think we can wrap it up. I'm sorry, page 3 of P02972. And if we could scroll to the bottom of that page with particular attention on the signature line. Mr. Jusic, do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Whose signature is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Delic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And after this issue -- order was issued, did the 35th and 37th divisions come into being?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 35th and the 37th Division had already been formed. This order should be understood as an order attempting to provide for some changes and corrections within the organisational structure. For example, the 319 was a part of the 35th Division. After this order, it was directly linked to the 3rd Corps command. And the Tesanj units were being re-established. Their designation was no longer 2 but rather 3, 317 and so on and so forth. As for item 6 on page 3, I wanted to stress its importance so as not to be misunderstood. That was the situation in January 1995. No. The order was issued in January 1995, and the period mentioned here was the deadline. In item 6 it says: "The written report of the implementation of task from this order shall be submitted to the general staff of the army be to the administration for the organisation and mobilisation of tasks at the latest by the 5th of March, 1995." Therefore, almost three months were envisaged for the implementation of this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a clarification. Perhaps it is important for the witness to clarify that with the Prosecutor. I don't know whether the Prosecutor wants to say that this chart is a part of this document to discuss now. I just want to know so that I can be able to prepare for my cross-examination. The chart shown, does it form an integral part of the signed document or not? Perhaps that can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, is the chart attached to that, as far as you know, a part of this original document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot state that. I don't remember exactly. I don't know whether the chart was attached to the document or not. In the document it says at the end: "Attachment is RF BH-100.201." I don't know what that means. I cannot recall exactly what it looked like at the time. According to me the attachment should be the war formation of BH-100.201. However, I cannot know exactly whether this chart was a part of this order or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess, Mr. Wood, you are going to have to be able to know what -- whether these are two separate documents, because you are going to tender them into evidence --.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and we have got to know what you are tendering in evidence. And are you going to be long on dealing with this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You deal with it and then we can take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: As to the chart, Mr. Jusic, does that chart accurately reflect the situation in the 3rd Corps in early part of 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. With the change I already mentioned concerning the line of command, it never went straight directly from the corps command to all of the other units, but it always goes through division commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time then, the Prosecution would seek to tender into evidence as two separate documents. I believe the testimony of the witness has established the authenticity or at least the accuracy of the information in the chart, and I believe the foundation has also been laid that this is an accurate document signed by Rasim Delic. At this time the Prosecution offers into evidence these documents separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When the Chamber refers to document P02972 being admitted, what does that refer to? Does it refer to the chart or to the order? And then how does -- how do we refer to the other document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, in the Prosecution's submission perhaps the other document given what's been said here should be given its own exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Having come in as what document from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Having come in as a part of P -- excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps what we could do here is assign the chart itself P02972A and the document P02972.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the document will be admitted into evidence as P02972. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 378.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the chart will come in as P02972A. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit number 379.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I see that it is an appropriate time for the break. This is also an appropriate time for the Prosecution to take a break, Your Honour, appropriate time in the examination, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Witness, before the break we were talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to apologise to both you and the witness. However, an issue came up concerning this document that needs to be discussed without the witness's presence, and I will explain to you once he leaves the courtroom. I don't think it would be wise for him to hear the argumentation as it might influence the rest of his testimony. This document has been admitted. However, I just wanted to direct your attention to a very serious matter in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will the witness please excuse us for a short while. Sorry about that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry that the day began on this note. I find myself in a position to keep interrupting, but there was one thing I noticed immediately once the document was pulled out and shown to the witness. It has been admitted into evidence as document 378. It is the same document that had been admitted as Exhibit 165. What I wanted to say is that there is a resurrection, if I may say, of another chart, the additional chart, and now this document is being tendered under a new number and presented to the Chamber. I am convinced that this was of no evil intent on the part of the Prosecution. However, this is a fabrication of sorts, especially since you admit these documents under a certain exhibit number. This is not the only case that I was able to see among the documents of the Prosecutor that they intend to use. I would kindly ask that the documents be used as a copy of the original. We shouldn't compile and put together documents by adding portions which do not belong to the original. Perhaps you can compare 165 and the one that the Prosecutor wanted to show you here today and present to you as a single document. I am very concerned with this pattern of behaviour, and I don't know what room it leaves me to control the fairness of this trial if we keep getting these compiled documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you sure, Madam Vidovic, that it is not tendered as separate exhibit from Exhibit 165 precisely because there is a difference between the attachments? Are you saying that in fact the covering document is exactly the same as the one that was tendered as Exhibit 165?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is exactly the same. It is the strictly confidential document of the General Staff. It is 4/19-3 of the 12th of January, 1995, admitted as Exhibit 165. The only difference is the ERN number of the Prosecution. This document, Exhibit 165, is completely identical to the one of today, 378, save for the unexpected appearance of the chart. I saw these documents as originals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have made that point, Madam Vidovic. All I wanted to know is was it not because there is this difference in the attachment. Let's hear what your opposite member has to say in response. Mr. Wood, are you able to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution had no intent to introduce the same exhibit twice. I did notice when I was preparing for this witness that this document was on the exhibit list twice. I didn't check to see whether it had been admitted under -- I think it was P01935. So I apologise for that, and the Prosecution has no objection to withdrawing one of these. Obviously there need not be two of them. But the Prosecution also believes that the chart stands on its own. As these things are gathered in archives, they're ERNed in a certain range and it was the Prosecution's understanding that this was an attachment to the document. But Prosecution also believes that even if it's not that this chart does stand on its own as a separate exhibit because the witness looked at it, and he said that this is the structure of the 3rd Corps as he recalls it in 1995. In that way, Your Honour, the Prosecution believes that this does stand on its own and that it can be given its own exhibit number. Again, the Prosecution has no intention to burden the record with duplicates of the same document, and we would with the Court's leave move to withdraw one of them. Certainly there need not be two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If in the document of January 1995 had a certain attachment under Exhibit 165, why does the attachment differ under Exhibit 378? That's the nub of the objection, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whether you can withdraw one of the two is neither here more there. The nub is whether -- is why the charts are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I can't explain that, Your Honour. I -- except to say that as these things, like you say, are gathered in the archives they're -- they're gathered together and then scanned and given an ERN range. When I looked at this document, it -- it seemed to me and I believe it was even ERNed that way, that the chart was a part of it, because the ERN is sequential. I can't say for certain whether that chart is a part of this order. But as I say, Your Honour, I believe that in a certain sense that's not a relevant point because the chart stands on its own as an accurate reflection of the 3rd Corps structure in 1995. As to why it's attached there, I can only surmise that it's because of the way it was gathered in the archive when the investigator went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think the problem is that when Exhibit 165 was admitted, it did not have any attachment. It was only the order of 12th January itself, and I suppose that the problem that the Defence has is now that suddenly this same exhibit pops up again now with an attachment, and so I understand the Defence's objection to imply that they're nervous about whether they get the whole story the first time the document is admitted. So the real reason that -- the real question is why wasn't the annex presented when this document was offered the first time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: That I'm not sure, Your Honour. As I said, there's -- there's a real possibility that these are two separate documents that were joined together through the investigation process when one was given a sequential ERN number to the order itself. The Prosecution does not believe that it detracts from the authenticity or the accuracy of the information in the 12 January order, and again both of those documents, each of them can stand on its own. Each has been admitted, and each is an accurate reflection, the witness has said, and plainly other witnesses have said, of the information from 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I just make a short intervention at this point, because I recall that some weeks ago I invited the parties to agree on a chart, if possible, showing the organisational structure of the 3rd Corps and the -- the connections or the relations between the 3rd and the 2nd Corps, and so obviously when this chart now pops up on our screens, my interest is to know whether this will comply with my invitation to the parties. Is this what I will get from my earlier invitation, or are the parties still working on agreements on what the organisational structure was of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution submits that this is a separate issue. I did not introduce this or show it to the witness with the intent of superseding or going beyond what the Trial Chamber had ordered. I showed this to the witness as a historical document, as a document that reflected the situation in 1995. That was done independently of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I look forward to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: -- the Chamber's invitations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- to your submissions. Thanks. Very briefly, Madam Vidovic, I seem to have understood you slightly differently from how Judge Harhoff understood you. I thought you said that there was an attachment to Exhibit 165, only the attachment differs from the attachment of today. Judge Harhoff seems to say that Exhibit 165 didn't have an attachment, but today there is an attachment. Which is the correct position? Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the understanding of Judge Harhoff is correct. Exhibit 165 did not have any attachments and now we do have an attachment with another exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any response to the explanation by the Prosecution as to how this may have happened and any suggestion as to how you think the Chamber should resolve the matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question seems to be cleared in my view now. However, the other document has not been exhibit -- or, rather, the attachment is not being exhibit as an integral part of the document. The reason why I wanted to draw your attention to this is a very serious one as you will see for yourselves. This is not the only document that will appear in this precise way. This is what I wanted to draw your attention to, as well as you -- and the Prosecutor's attention. They should be careful when showing copies of originals. They shouldn't compile any documents, but the copies should be true to the original. I have no objection to splitting these two documents and admitting them as such. As for any other issues, I can clear them with the witness during cross-examination. I believe it will become much clearer at that time. I hope I've answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except that there's a refrain that keeps coming up which is causing me concern. You suggest -- you're saying that you wanted to draw the attention to -- that you wanted that the Prosecution not to compile documents. I'm not quite sure what you mean by them compiling documents, Madam Vidovic. And you say that in relation to getting copies and not -- and not originals.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I'd like to say is the following: I will take Exhibit 965 as an example, and this has already been tendered. This was General Delic's order signed by him, and it ended here at the end of this document. This is what was disclosed to us as that document at the time. Either the Prosecutor at that time, as Judge Harhoff concludes, did not disclose the entire document as they should have, or somebody, not this Prosecutor but somebody from the OTP, annexed this appendix to this document which is not an integral part of that document, which is irregular. It is inappropriate, and it's worrying. At any rate, when I say that parties, not only the OTP but also the Defence, we have -- are duty-bound to present a copy of an original and stress that this is a document, but we should not add something that we should wish to see attached to this document as an attachment. This is what I wanted to relate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I gather -- the translation told us that you were referring to Exhibit 965. I want to believe you were referring to 378.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is Exhibit 965? We haven't reached 965 in our exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I referred to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 165. Okay. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. I heard you that you say you don't object to Exhibit 379 being tendered separately. I don't think there's any ruling that is required of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to withdraw 378 or 165?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution moves to withdraw Exhibit 165, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, the Prosecution wishes to withdraw 165. Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, let's see is how -- what -- what happens. But I would like to hear from the learned friend what they think this document is, whether that which was tendered under 165 or what they wanted to present to the witness today. I would like to hear from the learned friend what they think this document is, and for that reason I cannot accept or say that I'm satisfied at this moment with this proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why doesn't it satisfy you, Madam Vidovic? What are you asking for? Just in one sentence. Do you want -- we have -- we've got duplicates here of the same document as tendered as an exhibit. We obviously have to cancel one. Which one do you want to cancel?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, because of the future situations that may occur, I don't want to pre-judge anything, of course, but because of the possibility that in the future I may refer to certain issues of a fair trial, I would like this Exhibit 165 to remain as exhibit, and I want the 3 -- and a new number together with the attachment, 378 and 379, I wish both of them to remain as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I believe that for the sake of equity it would be better to withdraw the document which was tendered today, because otherwise we will be left with this ambiguity the regarding the -- this alleged document. So I think it would be adequate for the Prosecution to ask us to withdraw document 378.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I offer a third interpretation, because, Mr. Prosecutor, if you withdraw 165, it seems to me that implication of doing that is that actually the chart does belong to the order of 12 January. However, if you leave 165 as it is but withdraw 378, then the implication of that move is to suggest that the two documents have nothing to do with each other and that the chart stands for itself. So that's my first observation. And I understand that your move to withdraw 165 actually implies that you are of the opinion that the two documents always belonged together and that when the document was admitted way back as 165, it should have had had the chart but it didn't and that was a mistake. So now you move to have admitted the order as 378 with the attachment of the chart as 379. That's one issue. The other issue you is if we actually do remove Exhibit 165, then does that necessitate a renumbering all the exhibits from then up until now? In other words, if we end up removing 378, does the chart then become the new Exhibit 378?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Judge. I'm not getting any --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. My mistake. I didn't -- pressed the wrong button. The interpretation's mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get an interpretation of what was said so far.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Judge Lattanzi said "I should not agree that the exhibit tendered today," and then she will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the decision made today following the clarification provided by the prosecuting -- Prosecution according to which he thought, but he wasn't sure, this is my own interpretation, but he thought that the chart that was shown to us today was attached to the document, document which is actually a copy of Exhibit number 165, the decision made was not to admit it as an annexed document. So these are two separate documents. I think that this is not challenged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic has moved that both these exhibits stay, because as she says, she may have to refer to them later, and I think in fairness they should both stay, because -- I'm not quite sure whether -- what effect withdrawing any one of them will have on the testimony that was tendered about that document, because if they're withdrawn, then all the testimony that was tendered around that document must also be redacted, and I don't see how we can do that. So I tend to agree with Madam Vidovic, and I will rule, therefore, that both exhibits will stay. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may be seated, and once again I'm very sorry that we keep taking you in and out of the court. This is how things happen. Thank you very much for your understanding. You may proceed, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, as chief of staff of the 3rd Corps, what were your primary duties and functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood my functions as chief of staff as follows: They were not regulated to specifically anywhere, but on the basis of what I knew from my professional military upbringing and education and training and what was required by the circumstances of me to do. I was in charge of providing the training of the corps staff, to plan and to execute training of the corps. I was charged with regulating and controlling the level of training of my subordinate units, to control and maintain the battle readiness of subordinate units, to plan, organise the preparation for combat operations. And another major task was to organise the work and life in the command post. By this I mean the corps command. These would be the main tasks. Many others deriving from those major tasks, and of course the tasks handed down to me by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What was your role in respect of military security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Literally security is a separate department or sector which is directly connected to the commander, and this was so in formal in practical terms. I as chief of staff did not have, so to speak, any contact points nor any jurisdiction over the military security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what was your function in respect to military intelligence in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Military Intelligence Service was a separate entity within the corps command, in all corps commands, and in all other commands, and it was also directly connected to the commander in legal terms. It could be said that the chief of staff and assistants of the commander were in a way equal in their standing with regard to the commander, but the commander would relate or delegate certain powers to the chief of staff in the case of the absence of the commander, which means the chief of staff would regulate certain issues in the commander's absence, but these powers would be limited. And intelligence service was autonomous within the command of the corps. It was subordinated directly to the commander of the corps, had no contacts with me whatsoever apart from cases when combat operations were planned, when we would jointly prepare the combat plan and the orders. They would prepare their documents, and I as chief of staff, would take over their documents, and this was the very gist of our relationship. I could not change anything or alter anything in those documents and in their work, nor -- I could only highlight maybe some mistakes or something like at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: In practical terms, Mr. Jusic, how much of your time in 1995 in the 3rd Corps was devoted to planning operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time in 1995 we conducted, as far as I can remember, three major operations. One -- the first one planned by the corps command on the basis of an order by the General Staff. That was the lifting of the blockade of Sarajevo. The planning started in May, at the beginning of May. That operation was conducted, as far as I can remember, in June and July. The second operation, or second combat operation and the planning thereof, was work in conjunction work in conjunction with the 7th Corps to liberate Donji Vakuf. And the third operation in 1995 that I managed in terms of preparing the combat documents and preparation was the Farz operation to liberate Vozuca and to lift the blockade of the Zenica-Tuzla road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could ask you a few questions about these earlier operations. The operation to lift the blockade of Sarajevo, what was the outcome of that operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outcome was not a positive one. I think the 3rd Corps managed to liberate a part of an area from the -- in the region of Nabovic [phoen]. That's north-east of the town of Ilijas some 10 square kilometres. As a whole the operation was a failure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And as to the second operation you mentioned in conjunction with the 7th Corps, what was the outcome of that operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The operations aimed at liberating Donji Vakuf was started by the 7th Corps, and after the cessation of our operations around Sarajevo, after the failure there, the 3rd and 7th Corps started working together with -- towards Donji Vakuf, but that was unsuccessful as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So you mentioned this third operation devoted to liberating the Vozuca pocket. Is that the first such operation that is devoted to that military objective that you worked on, Mr. Jusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The operation to liberate Vozuca and to lift the blockade of the road, well, I was involved in that operation for the first time as chief of staff of the 3rd Corps. I organised the planning for that operation, and I took part directly in it. And this was the first time that I did so in capacity as chief of staff. There were previous combat operations along at that axis with the same objective, to improve the operational and tactical position of our units, and if possible the goal was to extend that target to lift the blockade of the road, but those operations were of limited success.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if -- if you recall, Mr. Jusic, when were these previous operations that you refer to aimed at the Vozuca pocket?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. Towards the Vozuca pocket. Hmm. Well, the label "Vozuca pocket" was adopted, but only the operations against the Vozuca-Zep -- or the Vozuca pocket continued throughout the war, from the beginning of the war, if we accept that defence actions of the BH army are also combat operations. These were aimed at improving the tactical and military position of our unit and with the possible aim of lifting the blockade, they started in 1994 and continued in 1995 until the beginning of the Farz operation. There were several of them. One of them was in July, at the time when the corps command was engaged in the operation aimed at lifting the siege of Sarajevo. That operation in June was the result, the fruit of the planning of the 35th Brigade command and the actions of its units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could have the witness shown please P02355.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you see that map on the screen before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And I realise it's -- it's not zoomed in very much, but in general terms can you tell the Court what this document is? And if you need to have it -- a closer look at any particular part, just let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could ask for the part to be zoomed in on the text "Odobravam" or "I approve."

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So for the record that would be the top left-hand corner of the document. If we could zoom in on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Top left corner. Could you zoom in on the list of units. It says here "Vozuca pocket." Slightly to the left. And could you zoom in on that slightly to the left towards the west and slightly lower. Lower. Towards the bottom. Towards the bottom. It is very difficult to see, but I know which document this is. This is a map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interrupt. The interpretation said can we zoom towards the west, and it looks like we went towards the east. No, go to the west. You are going to the east now. That's better. Is that what the witness wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, it's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know where --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Towards the top. I'm referring to the sides on the map. So we should move the map westwards. That means left on this monitor. And maybe slightly lower. Scroll towards the lower edge of the monitor. Even lower. I can't see is half of the pocket here. Yes. Now it's okay. No doubt this is the plan or the schematic of a decision by the commander of the 3rd Corps to conduct the Farz operation. This was prepared in the command of the 3rd Corps during the planning period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So if we could focus in on the bottom right-hand corner. And there's some text there. Can you tell the Court what that text is and what it means, Mr. Jusic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a standard procedure in the preparation of maps or in the preparation of plans on the maps whereby the commander of the corps, after the map had been prepared, and of course after an oral decision by him, that commander would sign the plan or the map, and would apply a rubber stamp of the corps. It was signed by the brigadier Sakib Mahmuljin as the commander, and of course his rubber stamp is attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court, sir, if you can, about that stamp? Who would be in possession of that stamp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the 3rd Corps command there were several rubber stamps. One small round rubber stamp was in the possession of the commander. A larger rubber -- round rubber stamp was in the -- in the trans -- sorry, in an office which would receive mail, documents, and certify them. Mainly all documents would go through this intake office, and the documents would be rubber stamped except for documents such as this one, a plan of combat operations, where the commander would apply the rubber stamp, or some documents personally prepared by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if we could zoom out again. A little bit more. Mr. Jusic, there's some text there in larger type or handwritten at the -- about the top third of the document. Can you tell the Court what that is and what it means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says: "Plan of attack operations of the 3rd Corps between the 10th of September until the 10th of October." There's no year, and the procedures did not provide for that. There was no need for the year to be mentioned. However, this map, as any other map, would always be accompanied by an order with a full date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And if we could focus finally on the top right-hand corner. I'm sorry, the top left-hand corner. There's some more handwritten text there. Could you tell the Court what that is and what effect it has on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to the standard procedures, this was the standard way to approve of a plan or a decision. The approval in this case, or as in every other case, is always done by a superior officer of the superior command. In this case it was commander army General Rasim Delic, who was in charge of the General Staff. That means that after all of the documents pertaining to the attacks have been reviewed by the various bodies of the General Staff, the Chief of the General Staff compiles a plan and then let's the commander know that everything is okay and that it can be signed. After the commander has signed, the plan is complete. What follows is the planning and actual preparation in order to implement the various aspects of the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Could the operation go forward without the signature of the commanding officer, in this scheme Rasim Delic -- in this case Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In an operation of such importance as this one could not have gone without his approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And how does a commander indicate his approval for going forward in an operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As part of the plans for an operation, there are many different documents, orders, and plans made by the competent bodies of the command covering different aspects of the operation. Those plans also envisaged the time of activities, their plan, and implementation, as well as taking up positions, reconnaissance, preparation. And also in the corps commander's order there should also be the date when the operation should begin. By signing this the commander of the General Staff approves all of the documentation as planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution offers into evidence, Your Honours, Exhibit P2 -- I'm sorry. Number P02355.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do so, Mr. Wood, and for the sake of completeness, can the witness also tell us what is written on -- in small print on the top right-hand corner of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is definitely something that can be put to the within. I believe that we do have a translation of all the text on this if I'm correct, on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but you have been asking him to tell us what is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- various text means but you haven't asked him about this, and I'm asking that you ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It's true. Just for Your Honours' sake, information, there will be a translation, but I'll put that to the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, can you tell us what the text in the box at the top right-hand corner of this document is and what it means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is also a part of the standard procedure when putting together a map or a plan. It says: "Defence of the Republic." It is clearly prescribed what a map should contain so that it would be complete. It says: "Defence of the Republic. Military secret," and the degree of secrecy is determined. It says here "Strictly confidential." In the armed forces there were various levels of secrecy. There was the official secret, the internal secret, the confidential, strictly confidential, and state military secret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Jusic. All we wanted to know is what is written here. Thank you so much. Okay. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, exhibit number 3880.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: One further question that I want to put to the witness about this exhibit, now exhibit, is Mr. Jusic, what does the "F" indicate in the box at the top right-hand corner of the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is precisely what I wanted to address. The "F" is short for Farz. It was the code-name of the operation that was approved by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusic. If we can zoom out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court, this has been admitted as an exhibit, but the Prosecution believes it will be helpful to have another copy of this map entered in as an exhibit once the witness has a chance to make certain markings on it to illuminate certain aspects that the Prosecution believes are important to this case. Just to advise the Court that I will ask him to make marks on this map at this point, but obviously the Prosecution wants the original map to be entered into evidence and it has now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jusic, if we can -- if we could have the map zoomed in a little bit. Sort of in the bottom third. That's good. Now, Mr. Jusic, can you explain to the Court what is meant by the dotted line that you see on the screen in front of you on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see three dotted lines. One of them in the middle on the tip of the pocket in the eastern part of the map moving straight up. It's a double dotted line with certain semi-circles in different spots. That was the line of separation between the zones of responsibility of the 3rd and 2nd Corps. It was the line of their competencies, including intelligence, security, and so on and so forth of two respective corps. That is one of lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, sir. But it might be helpful for the record if the witness be handed a pen so he can make that mark on the map to indicate the line of division between areas of responsibility between the 2nd and the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The line, 2nd and 3rd Corps from this point on. I think this elevation is called Krvavac. Should I continue with the line?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Jusic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically it went from the elevation called Krvavac through -- through the middle of the pocket to the top of Mount Ozren and further up to Doboj. That is the line of division. In this case, it means that it was also the line of the respective -- of the zone of responsibility of the 35th Division, since it was the unit to the north-east of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Okay. I'll ask you a little bit more about the 35th Division in a minute, but I believe it might be helpful to the Trial Chamber if you could indicate maybe in a different colour, in blue, perhaps, the border of what you're referring to as the Vozuca pocket, or explain what markings on the map that are on it now indicate what are the borders of the Vozuca pocket.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are such designations on the map. They are also marked with two dotted lines. The outside line to the east and to the west, the darker one. I think it should be blue. That is the front end the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The inside line that should be red represents the front end of the Chetnik forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood, which are these lines that the witness is talking about? He made one straight line, and now he's talking about lines and we don't know which lines he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I don't mean to put words in the mouth of the witness, Your Honour, but I believe what he's talking about is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. Ask him to mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask him to mark the different colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If you could, please, Mr. Jusic, to mark the ABiH lines in blue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this blue? To the north of Zavidovici, below the Blizna [phoen] facility or elevation, down to the Krivaja River towards Makorsko [phoen] hill and the hill called Krvavac. Then following the line of division to the 2nd Corps. These are the forces the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And right now I'm designating the forces of the 2nd Corps, and the line keeps going up northwards and to the east. This was the Vozuca pocket, this area here, was referred to as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be helpful if you could scroll the map up and you can continue that line for as long as it goes. Oh, I'm being told that's technologically not possible. So let the reflect, then, that the witness has marked the ABiH lines in blue and that he's marked the line of division between the 2nd and 3rd Corps in a vertical dotted line in red. Now, if -- yes. If -- if a different colour could be chosen, Mr. Jusic, I would like you to mark the VRS lines or the enemy's lines on the Vozuca pocket as you explained to the Court earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle the Chetnik lines were quite close to the lines of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The distance was between 300 and 5 or 600 metres. In certain places even less. Especially in this part here towards Opaljenik. I will complete the line of the Chetnik forces. This is their front end, their forward end. It represents the lines dug by both sides, the trenches, their fighting positions. In certain cases it would be used to attack, in others to defend. In addition to these lines there were some other elements in individual units which I need not designate right now. Those would refer to artillery positions, command positions, et cetera. The red line --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, the black line designates the Chetnik positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for our own clarification, you said the red line indicates what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I reply?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It represents the line of division of responsibility, the zones of responsibility between the 2nd and the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: So for the -- for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, then, this red line would have gone through the middle of the Vozuca pocket and essentially through what you would consider to be enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
